name: Linear vs Switching Supplies
title: Linear vs Switching Supplies
description: Linear supplies drop voltage as heat - simple, quiet, inefficient. Switching supplies chop and filter - efficient, complex, noisier. The choice trades efficiency against noise and simplicity.
how_it_works: Use linear where noise matters and current is low (precision analog, audio); use switching where efficiency matters (battery, high current). Size heatsinks for linear; follow layout rules for switching.
key_points: Linear: simple, low-noise, inefficient - best for low current.
Switching: efficient, complex, needs careful layout.
Heat is the linear supply's exhaust - heatsink it.
Choose by the load's needs, not by habit.

name: Voltage, Current, and Power Ratings
title: Voltage, Current, and Power Ratings
description: A supply must provide the load's voltage at its peak current with margin - and its power rating (volts x amps) must cover the worst case. Undersized supplies sag, overheat, and fail early.
how_it_works: Measure or calculate the load's peak current, add 20-30% margin, and choose a supply rated for at least that. Verify the rating is continuous, not peak, and check it at your operating temperature.
key_points: Voltage must match; current rating must exceed peak load plus margin.
Power rating = volts x amps at worst case.
Continuous ratings count; peak ratings mislead.
Derate for temperature - hot supplies deliver less.
requirements: Input source characteristics (voltage range, AC/DC); load requirements (voltage, current, ripple tolerance); safety standard for the product class.

name: Ripple and Noise

key_points: Ripple: residual AC; noise: high-frequency junk.
Sensitive loads need cleaner power than digital logic.
Measure at the load with proper scope technique.
Filter at the load; minimize noise at the source.
